query: For high-value components operating in aggressive environments, what intervention could improve surface physical and mechanical characteristics? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should remain effective, prior evidence that would support it, and an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Annealing a protective high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating on critical components will form a dense composite oxide layer through sluggish diffusion-enhanced selective oxidation, significantly improving the surface’s mechanical and physical properties in aggressive environments.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-value component (e.g., high-temperature steel) with an uncoated or conventionally coated surface that exhibits baseline wear, friction, and corrosion properties.
generation.intervention: Deposit an AlCrTiZrMo HEA thin film using Co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition (Co-FCVAD) and then anneal the coating at 800 °C for 1 hour.
generation.conditions: The component is used under aggressive service conditions, including high temperatures and corrosive/tribological environments, similar to those encountered in thermal shock and high-temperature oxidation scenarios.
generation.structural_mediator: The annealing process promotes the formation of a dense, protective ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface of the HEA film.
generation.mechanism: During annealing, selective oxidation of alloy constituents (especially Zr and Ti) controlled by the sluggish diffusion effect inherent to high-entropy alloys leads to the formation of a tightly adherent oxide layer that acts as a barrier against further oxidation and mechanical wear, thereby improving micro-scale hardness and reducing friction.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to an uncoated or unannealed baseline, the annealed HEA coating is expected to exhibit lower friction coefficients, reduced wear rates, and enhanced resistance to corrosive attack.
generation.baseline: Uncoated or as-deposited (unannealed) surfaces of similar components under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement is predicted to hold under conditions up to approximately 800 °C and in similar tribocorrosion environments; extreme conditions beyond these parameters may present uncertainties regarding long-term stability.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative benefits (e.g., percentage reduction in wear rate or COF) depend on coating uniformity, processing variations, and specific environmental factors. Further study is required to ascertain long-term cyclic thermal stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of test substrates: one set with the AlCrTiZrMo HEA thin film subjected to annealing at 800 °C for 1 hour and a control group with either no coating or the as-deposited coating without annealing. Subject both groups to identical high-temperature tribocorrosion tests using a linear reciprocating friction machine in a corrosive electrolyte, maintaining constant load, sliding frequency, and duration.
measurements: Surface morphology and phase analysis (using SEM and XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed HEA-coated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in COF, wear rate, and corrosion resistance relative to the uncoated or unannealed controls, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

In marine engineering, the materials of mechanical components need to have service reliability in extremely harsh working environments, that is, on the basis of excellent high-temperature mechanical properties, they must also have the ability to resist the erosion of oxygen or corrosive media in high-temperature environments. The oxidation, friction and corrosion of the materials of power components are the process of chemical or electrochemical reactions between the materials and the medium in the surrounding environment, which leads to the failure of the materials. Therefore, the development of protective coatings and the study of the effect of thermal shock on the performance of protective coatings are particularly important.
